pr.title: Remove early exits from JumpThreading.
pr.description:
This removes early exits from https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/131203 as I asked during review.

The correctness of the backtracking is `mutated_statement` clearing all relevant conditions. If `process_statement` fails to insert a new condition, for instance by const-eval failure, `mutated_statement`  still removes the obsolete conditions from the state.

pr.author: cjgillot

processing.reason: The PR only removes conservative early exits from JumpThreading; it does not introduce or fix a wrong-code transformation. Before the change, a failed local `process_statement` (const-eval/layout/mapping failure) propagated `None`, stopped the backwards traversal, and truncated that switch's collected `ThreadingOpportunity`s. After the change the traversal continues, relying on the unchanged `mutated_statement` flood/clearing invariant, so the difference is solely whether a valid optimization opportunity is retained. Both revisions are semantics-preserving for the source program, and the frozen analysis explicitly says this is an optimization/conservatism removal, not a confirmed miscompile and that no execution reproduction is claimed. A `test_program_pair` showing different printed values would therefore have to encode an unrelated rewrite or fabricate a miscompile, contrary to the requirement to encode only the actual historical wrong transformation. No source-grounded original/incorrect pair with differing runtime values can be validated.

analysis.originalLogic: Before this PR, JumpThreading's TOFinder used `Option<()>` as an error/abort channel throughout the backwards search. `start_from_switch` returned `Option<()>`; the driver saved `let old_len = finder.opportunities.len();` and, with the comment `// If we have any const-eval errors discard any opportunities found`, executed `if finder.start_from_switch(bb).is_none() { finder.opportunities.truncate(old_len); }`. Inside `find_opportunity`, `self.process_statement(bb, stmt, &mut state)?;` propagated any failure to the caller, and helper operations such as `eval_mir_constant(...).discard_err()?`, `try_eval_scalar_int(...)?`, `discriminant_for_variant(...).discard_err()?`, and `conditions.map(...)?` also returned `None`. Thus a local failure during processing a statement was treated as failure of the whole reverse traversal.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical behavior was over-conservative: when processing a statement failed to insert or transfer a condition (for example, a constant failed const-eval, layout lookup failed, a place was not tracked, or `unary_op`/`unary_op`-derived condition mapping failed), the finder propagated `None`, stopped scanning the remaining statements/predecessors, and the outer loop truncated all opportunities collected for that starting switch. It conflated "this one condition could not be registered" with "all opportunities discovered from this switch are invalid." The PR removes that failure-driven early exit and continues the traversal. This is an optimization/code-structure change, not evidence of a confirmed miscompile: the description grounds correctness in state cleanup rather than in the old abort: "The correctness of the backtracking is `mutated_statement` clearing all relevant conditions." In particular, "If `process_statement` fails to insert a new condition, for instance by const-eval failure, `mutated_statement`  still removes the obsolete conditions from the state." The unchanged early exits for `is_empty`, `MAX_COST`, `MAX_BACKTRACK`, loop headers, cleanup blocks, inline asm, etc. remain intentional.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR functions containing a `SwitchInt` whose discriminant can be mapped to a tracked place, with backward condition tracking over predecessor blocks/statements. The observable input region needs a multi-statement or multi-predecessor reverse traversal where at least one visited statement/operand cannot be processed locally (const-eval failure, failed layout, failed scalar-int conversion, failed discriminant evaluation, or untracked place), while another path/statement could still yield or extend a valid `ThreadingOpportunity`. A paired test can keep the same CFG and switch conditions, with one variant containing an unrelated const-eval-failing assignment/operand in the backwards path and the other replacing only that failing operation with an evaluable one; compare whether the valid switch opportunity survives. Also include a mutation of the tracked place after the failed insertion to exercise the state-clearing invariant.
analysis.summary: JumpThreading historically used `Option<()>` error propagation as control flow: any const-eval/layout/mapping failure while processing one backward condition aborted the search and truncated all opportunities from that switch. This merged PR removes those failure-driven early exits and continues searching, relying on `mutated_statement` to clear obsolete conditions. It is an optimization/conservatism removal, not a confirmed miscompile fix.
analysis.trigger: A `SwitchInt` traversal encounters a statement/operand that fails local processing (for example const-eval or layout/mapping failure), while other statements or predecessors in the same backwards search still contain a valid condition-target opportunity. Before the change the failure propagated as `None`, stopped traversal, and truncated the switch's opportunities; after the change traversal continues and the valid opportunity can be retained/threaded.
preconditions: JumpThreading runs on a MIR body with a `SwitchInt` terminator whose discriminant maps to a tracked place.
The backwards traversal has at least one locally unprocessable statement/operand, such as a MIR constant that fails const-eval, a failed `layout_of`, or an untracked place.
At least one other statement or predecessor can still register or extend a `ThreadingOpportunity` for the same starting switch.
`mutated_statement` still runs after `process_statement` and clears conditions for places mutated by the statement, even when condition insertion failed.
The unchanged limits (`is_empty`, `MAX_COST`, `MAX_BACKTRACK`) and loop-header/cleanup/inline-asm guards still apply; only failure propagation was removed.
pitfalls: Do not classify this as a proven miscompile fix: the historical behavior discarded valid optimization opportunities but the PR description does not claim wrong-code generation.
Do not assume ignoring a failed insertion is safe by itself; the stated invariant is that `mutated_statement` clears all relevant obsolete conditions from the state.
Do not remove the remaining intentional early stops (`is_empty`, cost/backtrack limits, loop headers, cleanup blocks, inline asm, unsupported switch forms).
Do not conflate a const-eval failure with a borrow/copy overwrite restriction; both affect tracked conditions but are separate causes.
A failed `process_statement` may have partially updated other state; tests should target the subsequent mutation-clearing behavior rather than assuming the failed condition was inserted.
analysis.testStrategy: Use rustc MIR-optimization tests (for example a `tests/mir-opt` JumpThreading snapshot) rather than claiming runtime reproduction. Construct paired MIR/Rust inputs with the same switch and CFG: variant A has an unrelated const-eval-failing assignment or operand in one backward path plus a valid switch opportunity elsewhere; variant B changes only that failing operation to an evaluable constant. Inspect the JumpThreading MIR dump/CFG snapshot and assert that the valid opportunity is retained/threaded after the change, whereas the old failure-propagation/truncation would drop it. Add a second case where the tracked place is overwritten after a failed insertion and verify the threaded path is not taken using stale conditions. Run MIR validation and the relevant mir-opt test suite; no execution or reproduction is claimed here.
